text:
On the evening of April 11, 1970, a Saturn V rocket lifted off from Kennedy Space Center carrying three men toward the Moon. Jim Lovell, the commander, had already flown on two Gemini missions and had orbited the Moon on Apollo 8. Fred Haise, on his first spaceflight, was the lunar module pilot. The command module pilot was Jack Swigert, who had been the backup until a few days before launch, when the prime crew member, Ken Mattingly, was pulled after being exposed to German measles. Swigert had trained for the mission alongside the others, so he stepped in without much disruption. Their destination was the Fra Mauro highlands, a landing site chosen for its geology.

The first two days went smoothly. The spacecraft drifted outward, the crew ran through their checklists, and on the evening of April 13, about fifty-five hours into the flight, Houston asked the crew to stir the cryogenic oxygen tanks in the service module. This was a routine procedure meant to keep the supercold oxygen and hydrogen mixed so that gauges would read accurately. Shortly afterward, the crew heard a loud bang and felt the spacecraft shudder.

Swigert radioed Mission Control with the sentence that became one of the most quoted lines in spaceflight: "Okay, Houston, we've had a problem here." Lovell later added, "Houston, we've had a problem. We've had a main B bus undervolt." Within minutes it was clear that an oxygen tank in the service module had ruptured. Investigators later traced the cause to wiring inside the tank. Years earlier, a thermostat had been designed for a higher voltage than the heater it controlled used, and the mismatch had damaged the wires' Teflon insulation. Stirring the tank had caused a short circuit, and the burning insulation ignited the oxygen. A second tank was soon lost as well, and the service module's fuel cells, which produced both electricity and drinking water from oxygen and hydrogen, were shut down.

The damage left the crew with a crippled ship and a serious problem. The command module Odyssey had only enough battery power to bring the crew home if it stayed switched off for most of the return. Flight director Gene Kranz and his team quickly decided that the lunar module Aquarius would serve as a lifeboat. Aquarius was built to support two men for about two days on the surface, not three men for four days in space. Its life-support systems, power, and water would have to stretch far beyond their design limits. The crew abandoned the command module, moved into the cramped lunar module, and began a long, cold, and wet journey.

The most urgent problem soon became carbon dioxide. The lunar module used round lithium hydroxide canisters to scrub CO2 from the air, but the command module's square canisters did not fit its receptacles. As the level rose, the crew faced a real risk of poisoning. In Houston, engineers were given the task of building an adapter from the materials available in the spacecraft. They worked through the night with a list of items the crew had on board, and the solution they arrived at used plastic bags, cardboard from a flight plan cover, duct tape, and a sock. Lovell and Haise assembled it under direction from the ground, and it worked well enough to keep the carbon dioxide at a safe level.

The crew then faced the task of getting home. Their route was a free-return trajectory, which would swing them around the far side of the Moon and fling them back toward Earth using the Moon's gravity, without needing a large engine burn. On April 14, a short burn of the lunar module's descent engine corrected the course. On April 15, the crew passed behind the Moon, about 254 kilometers above its surface, and they set a distance record for humans, roughly 400,000 kilometers from Earth. Being out of radio contact with Houston for about 34 minutes during the pass was a tense experience, and the spacecraft's systems were in a fragile state.

The return was cold and cramped. Temperatures inside Aquarius dropped low enough that the crew could see their breath, and water had to be rationed for a while. Mission Control set the reentry plan with extreme care, since the command module had been powered down and then had to be brought back online for reentry. Just before reentry, the crew jettisoned the damaged service module and photographed its shattered panels, a sight that made clear how close the mission had come to disaster.

On April 17, 1970, at 1:07 p.m. Eastern time, the command module Odyssey splashed down in the South Pacific, close to the recovery ship USS Iwo Jima. All three astronauts were alive and in good condition after nearly six days in space. The mission never landed on the Moon, but the response to the crisis became a model of engineering problem-solving and calm teamwork under pressure.

The story reached a wide audience through the 1995 film Apollo 13, directed by Ron Howard, and through Lovell's book Lost Moon, written with Jeffrey Kluger. The film dramatized several events and compressed others, but its central lesson held true: the mission succeeded because of ordinary people who kept thinking clearly when things went wrong.
